column1: What was the key structural defect of the Waterfall model identified as the root cause of software project failure?
column2: It assumed stakeholders could articulate complete, stable requirements before the software existed—a valid assumption for manufacturing known components, but catastrophically wrong for products whose value is discovered through use.

column1: According to the 1994 Standish Group CHAOS Report, what percentage of 8,380 IT projects were delivered on time and on budget?
column2: Only 16.2%. A further 31.1% were cancelled before completion, and the remainder were late, over budget, or missing promised features.

column1: What 1986 Harvard Business Review article inspired Scrum, and what core organizational pattern did it describe?
column2: Takeuchi and Nonaka's 'The New New Product Development Game.' It described companies like Honda and Canon using small, cross-functional teams with overlapping development phases instead of sequential hand-offs.

column1: What are the three pillars required for empirical process control to function in Scrum?
column2: Transparency (work and process visible to all stakeholders), Inspection (frequent checks to detect variance), and Adaptation (immediate adjustment when inspection reveals deviation).

column1: Which Scrum events map to each of the three empiricism pillars?
column2: Sprint = inspection container; Daily Scrum = daily inspection checkpoint; Sprint Review = inspection of the increment by stakeholders; Sprint Retrospective = inspection/adaptation of the team's own process.

column1: Why does the Definition of Done exist, and what is the core rule it enforces?
column2: It is a team-wide contract defining what constitutes a shippable, completed unit of work. A backlog item is either done or not done—there is no partial completion—preventing technical debt, scope creep, and velocity measurement error.

column1: What is Little's Law, and what does it state formulaically?
column2: CT = WIP / λ, where CT = average cycle time, WIP = average work-in-progress, and λ = average throughput. It is a proven mathematical identity holding across all stable queueing systems.

column1: According to Little's Law, what are the only two levers to reduce cycle time, and which is cheaper to implement?
column2: Reduce work-in-progress or increase throughput. Reducing WIP is a free, immediate policy decision; increasing throughput requires expensive, slow capacity expansion with diminishing returns.

column1: What is the core invariant that distinguishes Kanban's pull-based system from push-based methodologies?
column2: Work items enter the system only when capacity becomes available (pulled by demonstrated capacity), rather than being loaded according to a predetermined schedule (pushed by forecast).

column1: What common organizational instinct undermines Kanban flow efficiency, and why is it flawed?
column2: The instinct to maximize resource utilization by fully loading every worker with tasks. High utilization in a workflow system creates queueing delays that dwarf any efficiency gains from keeping workers constantly busy.

column1: What is the core invariant of single-team Agile success, and at what scale does it typically collapse?
column2: The ability to make autonomous decisions within a bounded domain where the team controls all dependencies needed to ship. It collapses beyond roughly five to seven interdependent teams, as coordination overhead grows combinatorially.

column1: What are the three predictable failure modes of naive Agile scaling?
column2: 1) Reversion to waterfall-style pre-coordinated quarterly planning due to dependency risk; 2) Conway's Law effects—architecture ossifies around org boundaries producing brittle APIs and duplicated services; 3) Velocity metrics become gaming targets (deferred integration, externalized tech debt, inflated estimates).
